1.Kesik Minare
A Roman temple converted into a Byzantine church and then a Seljuk mosque, the "Broken Minaret" was gutted by fire in 1800 and has since reopened for worship after a restoration that left its layered ruins on view.

2.Hıdırlık Tower
A 14-metre tower of tawny stone built by the Romans in the 2nd century CE, it stands where Kaleiçi meets Karaalioğlu Park and has served in turn as lighthouse, fortification, and lookout over the Gulf of Antalya.

3.Hadrian's Gate
A triumphal Roman arch raised in 130 CE to mark Emperor Hadrian's visit to the city, its three marble-columned archways form the only surviving entrance in Antalya's ancient walls.

4.Yivli Minare Mosque
An eight-grooved brick minaret raised by the Seljuk sultan Alaeddin Keykubad I in the 1230s, its fluted red-brick shaft traced with turquoise tile is the emblem most closely identified with Antalya.

Hibeş

Food Delivery
Getir
Foreign number: accepted. — sign-up takes an international prefix and the SMS code arrives without a Turkish SIM.
Turkey's fastest-growing app, covering both restaurant delivery and its own 10-minute grocery warehouses. The most reliable option for a foreign phone during a short stay.
getir.com
Yemeksepeti
Foreign number: not accepted. — the sign-up form only validates Turkish +90 mobile numbers.
Turkey's largest and longest-running delivery marketplace, with by far the widest restaurant selection in Antalya — but registration is blocked without a local SIM.
yemeksepeti.com
Trendyol Yemek
Foreign number: not accepted. — registration is restricted to Turkish mobile numbers, though guest checkout bypasses the phone field.
The delivery arm of Turkey's biggest e-commerce platform — strong restaurant and market coverage, best reached through guest checkout on a foreign phone.
tgoyemek.com

Getting Around
BiTaksi
Foreign number: accepted. — the SMS or WhatsApp code arrives on international numbers, though a booking is occasionally still refused as unavailable in the traveler's home country.
Turkey's most-used taxi app, hailing licensed metered taxis directly with fare and driver shown before pickup. The default way to book a ride without street-hailing.

Worth Knowing

One Stone, Four Empires

Day 1's four stops are really one story told in stone. Hıdırlık Tower went up under Rome, then did duty as a Byzantine lighthouse, a Seljuk watchtower, and an Ottoman lookout — the same 14 metres of masonry outliving four different rulers. Kesik Minare followed almost the identical arc a few hundred metres away: Roman temple, then Byzantine church, then Seljuk mosque, burned out, and only recently reopened as a mosque again. Nothing here was built once and left alone — it was re-covered and reused every time the city changed hands.

The 2-day loop and the water it revolves around share a hidden connection: the Düden River that surfaces at the upper falls on Day 2 spends 18 kilometres travelling underground first, vanishing into limestone sinkholes twice before it ever reaches daylight — and it still isn't finished, diving underground once more before finally throwing itself off a sea cliff at Lara, well outside this itinerary. What looks like two unrelated waterfalls in two different parts of the city is one river's very long, mostly invisible route to the Mediterranean.

Worth timing around: Antalya's biggest annual arts event fills a 2,000-year-old Roman theatre with opera and ballet every September, so a night at the show is often a realistic add-on to a September visit — not just a listing further down this page.
